Step 1 — payoffs and best responses
- You pick r (an integer 11–20). The other picks s.
- Your payoff = r + 20 * I(r = s − 1). So you get your request, and you get an extra $20 if you asked exactly one dollar less than the other player.
- For any fixed opponent choice s ≥ 12, your best pure response is r = s − 1 (since that yields r + 20 = s + 19, which is > 20 and > any r ≤ 20). If s = 11 you cannot play 10, so best response to 11 is 20.
- This creates a cycle of pure best responses (20 → 19 → 18 → … → 11 → 20), so there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium.

Step 2 — look for a symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium
- Let p_k be the probability the opponent requests k.
- If 20 is played with positive probability, the equilibrium expected payoff V must equal U(20) = 20.
- For any r with positive probability (11 ≤ r ≤ 19) we must have U(r) = r + 20·p_{r+1} = 20, so p_{r+1} = (20 − r)/20.
- If the support is contiguous from some T up to 20, these equalities determine p_{T+1},…,p_{20}, and p_T = 1 − sum_{k=T+1}^{20} p_k.

Step 3 — find the smallest T that gives a valid distribution
- Let n = 20 − T. Then sum_{k=T+1}^{20} p_k = (1/20)·(1 + 2 + … + n) = n(n+1)/40, so p_T = 1 − n(n+1)/40.
- We need p_T ≥ 0, so n(n+1) ≤ 40. The largest integer n satisfying that is n = 5 (because 5·6 = 30 ≤ 40, while 6·7 = 42 > 40). Thus T = 20 − 5 = 15.
- That gives a valid symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium with support {15,16,17,18,19,20}.

Step 4 — the equilibrium probabilities and payoffs
- From p_{r+1} = (20 − r)/20, we get:
  - p_20 = 0.05
  - p_19 = 0.10
  - p_18 = 0.15
  - p_17 = 0.20
  - p_16 = 0.25
- Then p_15 = 1 − (0.25+0.20+0.15+0.10+0.05) = 0.25.
- So the symmetric equilibrium mixed strategy is:
  - p_15 = 0.25, p_16 = 0.25, p_17 = 0.20, p_18 = 0.15, p_19 = 0.10, p_20 = 0.05.
- Any pure request in {15,16,17,18,19,20} yields the same expected payoff 20 against this distribution, and no lower request is profitable.

Conclusion — what to request
- In equilibrium any choice from 15 through 20 is optimal (equal expected payoff). A natural pure choice from the equilibrium support is 15.

We each choose an integer between 11 and 20. Your payoff equals the amount you request, plus a $20 bonus if your request is exactly $1 less than your opponent’s.

Best-response structure
- If the opponent requests x, then asking x − 1 (if allowed) gives payoff (x − 1) + 20 = x + 19, while asking any other r ≠ x − 1 yields payoff r.
- Since x + 19 > r for any r ≤ 20 when x − 1 is available, your best response to an opponent request x > 11 is x − 1.
- If the opponent requests 11, you cannot ask 10, so the best you can do then is 20.
This produces a cycle of pure best responses (11 → 20 → 19 → 18 → ... → 12 → 11), so there is no pure-strategy Nash equilibrium. We must look for a symmetric mixed-strategy equilibrium.

Set up a symmetric mixed equilibrium
Let p_k be the probability the opponent requests k. The expected payoff from choosing k is
U(k) = k + 20 · p_{k+1} (with p_{21} = 0).
In a symmetric equilibrium, every pure strategy used with positive probability must give the same expected payoff v. Suppose the support of the equilibrium is the consecutive set {a, a+1, …, b}. For k in that support:
v = k + 20 · p_{k+1}.
If b is the top of the support then p_{b+1} = 0, so v = b. Thus for k = a, a+1, …, b − 1 we have
p_{k+1} = (b − k) / 20,
i.e. p_{a+1} = (b − a)/20, p_{a+2} = (b − a − 1)/20, …, p_b = 1/20.
The leftover probability mass is p_a = 1 − sum_{j=a+1}^{b} p_j. All p_j must be nonnegative.

Feasible supports
Since any k > b would yield U(k) = k > b = v, b must be the maximum allowed value 20. So b = 20. With b = 20 and support {a, …, 20}, the probabilities for j = a+1..20 are (21 − j)/20 and
sum_{j=a+1}^{20} p_j = (1/20)·(20−a)(21−a)/2.
We need p_a = 1 − that sum ≥ 0, which requires (20−a)(21−a) ≤ 40. The largest interval satisfying that is a = 15 (since for a = 15 we get (5)(6) = 30 ≤ 40, and for a = 14 we get 6·7 = 42 > 40). So the equilibrium support is {15,16,17,18,19,20}.

Compute the equilibrium probabilities
For a = 15:
- p15 = 1 − (1/20)·(1+2+3+4+5) = 1 − 15/20 = 0.25
- p16 = 5/20 = 0.25
- p17 = 4/20 = 0.20
- p18 = 3/20 = 0.15
- p19 = 2/20 = 0.10
- p20 = 1/20 = 0.05

Check indifference: for k = 15..20,
U(k) = k + 20·p_{k+1} = k + 20·((21 − (k+1))/20) = k + (20 − k) = 20,
so every strategy in the support yields expected payoff 20. Any k < 15 yields U(k) < 20, so no profitable deviation.

Conclusion and choice
In the symmetric Nash equilibrium of this one-shot game, you randomize over {15,16,17,18,19,20} with the probabilities above. All of those choices give the same expected payoff (20), and 15 is one of the equilibrium pure requests and has the largest single probability among the allowed values (tied with 16).
